title: Look before you copy
story: Seirawan recalls copying his opponent instead of examining the position. Replaying the game reveals a free bishop that he missed. Before following a plan, check what the last move changed.
prompt: White to move. Win the unprotected bishop.
hints: Look for a capture before copying a move.
The queen has an open diagonal from d1.
question: What should you do after your opponent moves?

title: Check is not checkmate
story: The same childhood game ended with a mistaken claim of checkmate. The king was in check, but several legal blocks were available. An uncomfortable position is not automatically a lost game.
prompt: White is in check. Block the bishop’s attack.
hints: Check the diagonal from b4 to e1.
A piece or pawn can block on c3 or d2.
question: When is a checked king checkmated?
choices: When no legal move removes the check

title: Keep the rooks safe
story: Seirawan imagined his rooks as cannons and brought them out before his other pieces. A bishop captured a rook. Even after a mistake, examine the position for the best recovery.
prompt: White has lost a rook. Capture the bishop in return.
hints: Do not ignore a capture just because your plan went wrong.
The knight on g1 can recapture.
question: What is the useful response when your plan fails?

title: Develop with a threat
story: After an early queen capture in the Scandinavian Defense, White can develop a knight while attacking the queen. This gains time for development. Early queen moves are not always wrong; their cost depends on the position.
prompt: Develop a knight and attack the black queen.
hints: Can one move do two useful jobs?
The knight on b1 can reach c3.
question: What does developing with tempo mean here?

title: Meet the queen raid
story: A queen and bishop aimed at f7 can threaten a quick mate. In the book’s example, Black first defends the e5-pawn, then blocks the mating threat while attacking the queen.
prompt: Black to move. Block the queen’s path to f7 and attack her.
hints: The black knight already protects e5.
A pawn can move from g7 to g6.
question: Why does the position matter before pushing the g-pawn?
choices: Other threats, including e5, must be covered

title: Bring another defender
story: The raiding queen renews the threat from f3. Black calmly develops another minor piece. Coordinated development can make a queen attack lose time.
prompt: Black to move. Develop a knight to block the attack on f7.
hints: Find the line between f3 and f7.
The g8-knight can move to f6.
question: What makes this defence useful?
choices: It develops a piece and answers the threat

title: Make room in the centre
story: Chapter 2 puts pawns and minor pieces at the heart of opening play. A central pawn move can claim space and open lines for development. The four central squares are d4, e4, d5 and e5.
prompt: White to move. Advance a central pawn two squares.
hints: Choose the d-pawn or e-pawn.
Either d4 or e4 meets this lesson’s goal.
question: Which group contains the four central squares?

title: Develop with purpose
story: The book describes learning to bring knights and bishops into the game before launching queen or rook adventures. Choose useful squares, watch threats, and coordinate your pieces.
prompt: White to move. Develop a knight toward the centre.
hints: Both knights have useful central developing squares.
Nf3 attacks e5; Nc3 supports e4 and controls d5.
question: Which pieces usually take priority in opening development?

title: Give the bishop a job
story: In the illustrative game, White brings a bishop to c4, developing it while eyeing f7. Development is most useful when a piece helps a concrete plan.
prompt: Develop the f1-bishop to aim at f7.
hints: Look along the diagonal leading to f7.
The bishop can move to c4.
question: What makes c4 purposeful for this bishop?
choices: It develops while pointing at f7

title: Give your king shelter
story: The book’s opening goal is a safe king and a playable middlegame. This original practice position applies that principle: White has cleared the kingside and can castle legally.
prompt: White to move. Castle kingside to improve king safety.
hints: Castling moves the king and rook together.
Select the king on e1, then g1.
question: Which condition prevents castling?
choices: Your king would cross an attacked square

title: Pieces working together
story: In the book’s Legall’s Mate example, Black takes the queen and overlooks the coordinated minor pieces. The lesson is to calculate forcing moves rather than judge a position by material alone.
prompt: White to move. Find the forcing check, then finish the mate.
hints: Look for a bishop check on f7.
After the king moves to e7, bring the c3-knight to d5.
question: Why is losing the queen acceptable in this example?

title: Learn from the game
story: Seirawan explains how recording games, analysing them and playing stronger opponents helped him improve. Review a familiar position and identify a useful move for yourself. The next step is to apply these principles in real games.
prompt: Develop your f1-bishop to an active square: c4 or b5.
hints: Bring a new piece into play.
Bc4 aims at f7; Bb5 pressures the defender on c6.
question: What should you do after a difficult loss?
choices: Review the moves and identify a lesson
